topics.title: Transverse and longitudinal waves; frequency, wavelength, amplitude and the wave equation

cards.front: What do all waves do, and how?
cards.back:
They **transfer energy** from one point to another **through vibrations**.

The medium itself is not carried along with the wave.

cards.front: Define a transverse wave
cards.back:
A wave in which the particles vibrate **perpendicular to the direction of wave travel** (at right angles to it).

Water waves and all electromagnetic waves are transverse.

cards.front: Define a longitudinal wave
cards.back:
A wave in which the particles vibrate **parallel to the direction of wave travel**.

Sound and ultrasound are longitudinal.

cards.front: Trap: is sound transverse or longitudinal?
cards.back:
**Longitudinal** - and so is ultrasound.

Calling sound transverse is a repeated error in the reports. Only water waves and electromagnetic waves are named as transverse on this specification.

cards.front: Define the wavelength of a wave
cards.back:
The distance between **two neighbouring crests (or troughs)** of a transverse wave, or between **two neighbouring compressions** of a longitudinal wave.

Measured in metres.

cards.front: Define the frequency of a wave
cards.back:
The **number of waves produced each second** by the source, or the number passing a point each second.

Measured in hertz (Hz).

cards.front: Define the amplitude of a wave
cards.back: The **maximum displacement of a particle from its undisturbed position** - measured from the rest line to a crest, never from a crest to a trough.

image.alt: A transverse wave drawn about a dashed rest position line, with the wavelength marked between two successive crests and the amplitude marked from the rest line up to a crest.
image.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 152' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.5'><path d='M20 82 L300 82' stroke-width='1' stroke-dasharray='4 4'/><path d='M20 82 Q55 22 90 82 Q125 142 160 82 Q195 22 230 82 Q265 142 300 82'/><path d='M55 40 L195 40' stroke-width='1'/><path d='M61 36 L55 40 L61 44 M189 36 L195 40 L189 44' stroke-width='1'/><path d='M195 82 L195 54' stroke-width='1'/><path d='M191 60 L195 52 L199 60' stroke-width='1'/><g font-size='9' fill='currentColor' stroke='none'><text x='96' y='34'>wavelength</text><text x='202' y='72'>amplitude</text><text x='22' y='102'>rest position</text></g></svg>

cards.front: Equation for the speed of a wave
cards.back:
In words: wave speed = frequency x wavelength.

In symbols: $v = f\lambda$

Units: v in m/s, f in Hz, $\lambda$ in m.

Rearranged: $f = \frac{v}{\lambda}$ and $\lambda = \frac{v}{f}$. Convert kHz and MHz to Hz, and cm to m, first.

cards.front: Equation linking frequency and period
cards.back:
In words: frequency = 1 divided by the period (the time for one complete wave).

In symbols: $f = \frac{1}{T}$

Units: f in Hz, T in s. Rearranged: $T = \frac{1}{f}$.

Use it to read a frequency off a displacement-time graph.

cards.front: Trap: one complete wave takes 2 s. Is the frequency 2 Hz?
cards.back:
**No - it is 0.5 Hz.** $f = \frac{1}{T} = \frac{1}{2}$.

A period of 2 s means only half a wave is made each second. Examiners flagged exactly this confusion at Higher Tier.

topics.title: Echoes, ultrasound, sonar and radar

cards.front: Equation for the distance to a reflector from an echo
cards.back:
In words: distance = (speed x time) divided by 2.

In symbols: $d = \frac{vt}{2}$

You halve because the sound travels **there and back** in that time. Units: d in m, v in m/s, t in s.

cards.front: An echo returns from a cliff after 0.4 s. The speed of sound is 340 m/s. Distance to the cliff?
A sonar pulse takes 0.06 s to return from the seabed. Sound travels at 1500 m/s in water. Depth?
Define ultrasound
cards.back: Sound that has a **frequency above 20 000 Hz** - higher than a human ear can hear.

cards.front: Give the medical and the industrial use of ultrasound named in this specification
cards.back:
**Medicine**: measuring the diameter of a foetus's head in a pregnancy scan.

**Industry**: detecting defects (cracks and flaws) inside metals.

cards.front: What does sonar use, and what for?
cards.back: **Sound pulses** sent through water, to detect objects under water such as the seabed, shoals of fish or wrecks.

cards.front: What does radar use, and what for?
cards.back:
**Electromagnetic waves** (radio and microwaves), to detect aircraft and ships.

They travel through air and space, where sound cannot be used.

cards.front: Trap: an echo question gives the time as 500 ms and you divide by two at the wrong moment. What is the safe order?
cards.back:
1 Convert the time to seconds (500 ms = 0.5 s).
2 Work out the **total** path: speed x time.
3 **Then** halve it, because the wave went out and came back.

topics.title: The electromagnetic spectrum and its dangers

cards.front: List the electromagnetic spectrum in order of increasing frequency
cards.back:
Radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays.

That is also the order of **decreasing wavelength**.

cards.front: How do the speeds of the different electromagnetic waves compare in a vacuum?
cards.back:
They all travel at the **same speed** in a vacuum.

Only their frequency and wavelength differ.

cards.front: Across the electromagnetic spectrum, as the frequency increases the wavelength ____.
cards.back:
**decreases**

The speed is fixed in a vacuum, so $v = f\lambda$ means a higher frequency must come with a shorter wavelength.

cards.front: Trap: 'microwaves are dangerous because they heat you up'. What is missing?
cards.back:
The word **internal**: microwaves cause **heating of internal body tissue**.

Examiners specifically required the danger to be linked to tissue inside the body.

cards.front: What harm do infrared and intense visible light do?
cards.back:
**Infrared** is felt as heat and causes **skin burns**.

**Intense visible light** damages the **eyes**.

cards.front: What harm does ultraviolet radiation do?
cards.back: Certain wavelengths of ultraviolet **damage skin cells** and can lead to **skin cancer**.

cards.front: What harm do X-rays and gamma rays do?
cards.back: They **damage cells**, and that damage may lead to **cancer**.

cards.front: What is the general rule linking frequency and danger?
cards.back:
The **higher the frequency** of the radiation, the **more damage** it is likely to do to the body.

That is why gamma rays are the most hazardous region and radio waves the least.

topics.title: Reflection in a plane mirror

cards.front: Where are the angles of incidence and reflection measured from?
cards.back:
From the **normal** - a construction line drawn **at right angles to the mirror** at the point where the ray strikes it.

The normal is drawn as a dashed line.

image.alt: A ray of light striking a plane mirror, with a dashed normal drawn at right angles to the mirror at the point of incidence. The angle of incidence i and the angle of reflection r are both marked between the rays and the normal.
image.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 300 166' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.5'><path d='M40 112 L260 112' stroke-width='2.5'/><path d='M50 112 L40 124 M74 112 L64 124 M98 112 L88 124 M122 112 L112 124 M146 112 L136 124 M170 112 L160 124 M194 112 L184 124 M218 112 L208 124 M242 112 L232 124' stroke-width='1'/><path d='M150 112 L150 22' stroke-width='1' stroke-dasharray='4 4'/><path d='M62 30 L150 112'/><path d='M110 75 L100 71 L106 65 Z' fill='currentColor' stroke='none'/><path d='M150 112 L238 30'/><path d='M198 67 L194 77 L188 71 Z' fill='currentColor' stroke='none'/><g font-size='9' fill='currentColor' stroke='none'><text x='130' y='80'>i</text><text x='160' y='80'>r</text><text x='154' y='20'>normal</text><text x='212' y='138'>mirror</text></g></svg>

cards.front: State the law of reflection
cards.back: The **angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection**.

cards.front: Trap: a ray meets a mirror at 20 degrees to the mirror surface. What is the angle of incidence?
cards.back:
**70 degrees** (90 - 20).

Angles are always measured from the **normal**, not from the mirror, so subtract from 90 whenever the question gives the angle to the surface.

cards.front: Describe the image seen in a plane mirror
cards.back: **Same size** as the object, **upright**, **laterally inverted** (left and right swapped), **virtual**, and **as far behind the mirror as the object is in front**.

cards.front: Define a virtual image
cards.back: An image the rays only **appear** to come from - they never actually meet there, so it **cannot be caught on a screen**.
keyWords: cannot be formed on a screen

cards.front: A ray strikes a plane mirror at 35 degrees to the normal. Angle of reflection?
cards.back:
**35 degrees**

The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.

cards.front: A girl stands 1.5 m in front of a plane mirror. How far is she from her image?
cards.back:
**3 m**

The image is 1.5 m behind the mirror, so the object-to-image distance is 1.5 + 1.5 m.

cards.front: Locate the image in a plane mirror by ray tracing
cards.back:
1 Draw two rays from a point on the object to the mirror.
2 Draw the normal at each point and reflect each ray with i = r.
3 Continue both reflected rays away from the mirror.
4 Extend them **backwards** behind the mirror as **dashed** lines.
5 The image point is where the dashed lines cross.

topics.title: Refraction and dispersion

cards.front: Which way does light bend on entering glass, and which way on leaving it?
cards.back:
It bends **towards the normal** when it enters glass or water, because it **slows down**.

It bends **away from the normal** when it leaves and speeds up again.

image.alt: A ray of light entering a rectangular glass block from the upper left. Dashed normals are drawn at right angles to the surfaces at the entry and exit points. Inside the glass the ray bends towards the normal, and on leaving it bends away from the normal, emerging parallel to the original ray.
image.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 330 180' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.5'><rect x='90' y='60' width='150' height='60'/><path d='M120 34 L120 92' stroke-width='1' stroke-dasharray='4 4'/><path d='M150 88 L150 152' stroke-width='1' stroke-dasharray='4 4'/><path d='M70 36 L120 60'/><path d='M100 51 L90 50 L93 43 Z' fill='currentColor' stroke='none'/><path d='M120 60 L150 120'/><path d='M138 95 L130 88 L137 85 Z' fill='currentColor' stroke='none'/><path d='M150 120 L200 150'/><path d='M180 138 L170 136 L174 130 Z' fill='currentColor' stroke='none'/><g font-size='9' fill='currentColor' stroke='none'><text x='124' y='30'>normal</text><text x='154' y='164'>normal</text><text x='104' y='54'>i</text><text x='126' y='80'>r</text><text x='168' y='96'>glass block</text><text x='44' y='58'>air</text></g></svg>

cards.front: Trap: 'the ray bends because glass is more optically dense'. Why is that not enough?
cards.back:
Refraction must be explained by a **change of speed**: the light **slows down** in glass, so it bends towards the normal.

The examiner's report says the explanation must be a speed change, not 'optical density'.

cards.front: What decides how much a ray is refracted?
cards.back:
The **size of the change of speed**: the greater the change of speed, the greater the refraction.

Snell's law is not required on this specification.

cards.front: Define dispersion
cards.back: The **splitting up of white light into its different colours**.

cards.front: Define a spectrum
cards.back: The **range of colours** produced when white light undergoes **dispersion**.

cards.front: Trap: a prism splits white light. Is that refraction, and is the result a rainbow?
cards.back:
Call the process **dispersion** (refraction is the bending of a single ray) and call the result a **spectrum**, not a 'rainbow'.

Both words were penalised in Summer 2025.

cards.front: Why does a prism split white light into a spectrum?
cards.back: The different **colours travel at different speeds in the glass**, so each colour is refracted by a different amount and they separate.

cards.front: Which colour is refracted least by a prism, and which most?
cards.back:
**Red** is refracted the least, because it is **slowed the least** in the glass.

**Violet** is refracted the most, because it is slowed the most.

cards.front: Prescribed Practical P5: measuring angles of incidence and refraction with a glass block
cards.back:
1 Draw round the block and mark where the ray enters.
2 Draw the **normal** there with a protractor.
3 Mark the incident and emerging rays with pairs of pins.
4 Remove the block, join the marks and measure i and r **from the normal**.
5 Repeat over the full range of angles, leaving no gaps, and plot i against r.
cards.source: Prescribed Practical P5; CER Summer 2025 U7B Physics

cards.front: What does the graph of angle of incidence against angle of refraction show?
cards.back:
The two angles are **related but not proportional**.

The graph is a **curve**, not a straight line through the origin - directly proportional would need both.
cards.source: Prescribed Practical P5; CER Summer 2025 U7A Physics

cards.front: Trap: a ray is drawn through a prism with no normals. What usually goes wrong?
cards.back:
Without the **normal at each surface** the ray is almost always bent the **wrong way**.

Draw the normal first, then decide: slowing down bends the ray towards it, speeding up bends it away.

topics.title: Converging and diverging lenses; measuring focal length

cards.front: What does a converging lens do to rays that arrive parallel to the axis?
cards.back:
It **brings them together** at a single point on the axis - the **principal focus**.

A converging (convex) lens is fatter in the middle than at its edges.

cards.front: What does a diverging lens do to rays that arrive parallel to the axis?
cards.back:
It **spreads them out**, so they appear to come from a point on the near side of the lens.

A diverging (concave) lens is thinner in the middle than at its edges.

cards.front: Trap: how do you tell a converging lens from a diverging lens in a diagram?
cards.back:
**Converging: fat in the middle** and it brings rays together.
**Diverging: thin in the middle** and it spreads rays out.

A significant minority of candidates swap the two names.

cards.front: Define the focal length of a converging lens
cards.back: The distance between the **principal focus** and the **centre of the lens**.

cards.front: Measure the focal length of a converging lens using a distant object
cards.back:
1 Face the lens towards a **distant object**, such as a window or a tree.
2 Hold a screen behind the lens.
3 Move the screen until the image on it is **sharply focused**.
4 Measure the distance from the **centre of the lens to the screen** with a ruler.
5 That distance is the focal length; repeat and take a mean.

cards.front: Why does the distant-object method give the focal length?
cards.back:
Rays arriving from a very distant object are effectively **parallel** to the axis, so the lens brings them to a focus **at the principal focus**.

The screen is then one focal length from the lens.

cards.front: Trap: a ray diagram loses a mark for the focal point. What is expected?
cards.back:
**F must be labelled on the axis on both sides of the lens**, each one focal length from the centre.

Examiners report that candidates did not know where to put the label.

cards.front: Rays arriving parallel to the axis of a converging lens all pass through the ____ ____ after the lens.
cards.back: **principal focus**

topics.title: Ray diagrams for converging lenses: camera, projector and magnifying glass

cards.front: Draw the three standard rays from the top of an object through a converging lens
cards.back:
1 A ray **parallel to the axis**, which is refracted **through F** on the far side.
2 A ray **through the centre of the lens**, which carries straight on undeviated.
3 A ray **through F on the object side**, which leaves **parallel to the axis**.

All three cross at the top of the image.

image.alt: A ray diagram for a converging lens with an object arrow beyond 2F on the left. Three rays are drawn: one parallel to the axis then through F, one straight through the centre of the lens, and one through F then parallel. They cross between F and 2F on the right, where a shorter inverted image arrow is drawn.
image.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 156' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.5'><path d='M16 90 L306 90' stroke-width='1'/><path d='M160 44 Q178 90 160 136 Q142 90 160 44 Z'/><path d='M110 85 L110 95 M210 85 L210 95 M60 85 L60 95 M260 85 L260 95' stroke-width='1'/><path d='M40 90 L40 60'/><path d='M36 66 L40 58 L44 66' /><path d='M40 60 L160 60 L270 126'/><path d='M40 60 L270 118'/><path d='M40 60 L160 111 L270 111'/><g fill='currentColor' stroke='none'><path d='M106 60 L98 56 L98 64 Z'/><path d='M115 79 L106 80 L108 74 Z'/><path d='M105 88 L96 88 L99 81 Z'/><path d='M219 96 L211 95 L214 88 Z'/><path d='M221 111 L213 107 L213 115 Z'/></g><path d='M246 90 L246 111'/><path d='M242 105 L246 113 L250 105'/><g font-size='9' fill='currentColor' stroke='none'><text x='106' y='106'>F</text><text x='206' y='106'>F</text><text x='52' y='106'>2F</text><text x='266' y='106'>2F</text><text x='16' y='52'>object</text><text x='244' y='132'>image</text></g></svg>

cards.front: Where is the image on a lens ray diagram?
cards.back:
Where the **refracted rays cross**. Draw the image as an arrow from the axis up (or down) to that crossing point.

Two rays are enough to fix it; a third is a useful check.

cards.front: Trap: your rays are in exactly the right places but marks are still lost. What is missing?
cards.back:
**Direction arrows on every ray.**

Missing arrowheads are named in report after report as a lost mark on otherwise correct diagrams.
cards.source: CER Summer 2024 P2 (F); CER Summer 2025 P2 (H)

cards.front: Trap: a scale ray diagram is drawn on a grid. What two things must be read off it?
cards.back:
The **distance of the image from the centre of the lens** and the **height of the image**, both counted off the grid squares.

Marks are given for an image at the correct position and size, not just for the rays.
cards.source: CER Summer 2023 P2 (H); CER Summer 2025 P2 (F)

cards.front: Define a real image
cards.back:
An image formed where the refracted rays **actually meet**, so it **can be caught on a screen**.

In a converging lens a real image is always **inverted**.

cards.front: Define a virtual image formed by a lens
cards.back:
An image the rays only **appear to come from** when they are extended backwards, so it **cannot be caught on a screen**.

It is upright and on the same side of the lens as the object.
keyWords: cannot be formed on a screen

cards.front: An object is placed beyond 2F from a converging lens. Describe the image.
cards.back:
**Real, inverted and diminished**, formed between F and 2F on the other side.

This is the arrangement used in a **camera**.

cards.front: An object is placed between F and 2F from a converging lens. Describe the image.
cards.back:
**Real, inverted and magnified**, formed beyond 2F on the other side.

This is the arrangement used in a **projector**.

cards.front: Higher: an object is placed inside F. Describe the image.
cards.back:
**Virtual, upright and magnified**, on the **same side of the lens as the object**.

This is the **magnifying glass**. Find it by extending the refracted rays backwards as dashed lines.

image.alt: A ray diagram for a magnifying glass. A short object arrow stands between F and the converging lens. One ray parallel to the axis is refracted through F, and one passes straight through the centre. Both are extended backwards as dashed lines, meeting at a taller upright virtual image on the same side as the object.
image.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 300 150' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.5'><path d='M12 90 L290 90' stroke-width='1'/><path d='M160 48 Q177 90 160 132 Q143 90 160 48 Z'/><path d='M100 85 L100 95 M220 85 L220 95' stroke-width='1'/><path d='M120 90 L120 75'/><path d='M117 79 L120 73 L123 79'/><path d='M120 75 L160 75 L280 105'/><path d='M120 75 L250 124'/><g fill='currentColor' stroke='none'><path d='M146 75 L138 71 L138 79 Z'/><path d='M225 91 L216 93 L218 86 Z'/><path d='M205 107 L196 107 L198 101 Z'/></g><path d='M160 75 L40 45 M120 75 L40 45' stroke-width='1' stroke-dasharray='4 3'/><path d='M40 90 L40 45'/><path d='M36 51 L40 43 L44 51'/><g font-size='9' fill='currentColor' stroke='none'><text x='96' y='106'>F</text><text x='216' y='106'>F</text><text x='112' y='120'>object</text><text x='6' y='36'>virtual image</text></g></svg>

cards.front: Trap: why does 'the image is real, virtual and upright' score zero?
cards.back:
It **contradicts itself**, and a correct word beside an incorrect one scores nothing.

Choose **one** word from each pair: real or virtual, upright or inverted, magnified or diminished.

cards.front: How does a simple camera use a converging lens?
cards.back:
The object is **beyond 2F**, so the lens forms a **real, inverted, diminished** image on the film or sensor, which acts as the screen.

The lens is moved to focus objects at different distances.

cards.front: How does a projector use a converging lens, and why is the slide put in upside down?
cards.back:
The slide sits **between F and 2F**, so the image on the screen is **real, magnified and inverted**.

The slide is loaded upside down so that the inverted image appears the right way up.

cards.front: Trap: how would you actually view the real image formed by a converging lens?
cards.back:
Put a **screen** where the rays cross - a real image can be caught on a screen.

Only a small minority realised this; a virtual image could not be shown that way.

topics.title: Conductors, insulators, current direction, circuit symbols and cell polarity

cards.front: What is the difference between a conductor and an insulator?
cards.back:
A conductor has **free electrons** that can move through it and carry a current.

An insulator has **no free electrons**, so charge cannot flow.

cards.front: In which direction do the electrons move, and in which direction is the conventional current?
cards.back:
The **electrons** flow from the **negative** terminal to the **positive** terminal.

**Conventional current** is drawn the opposite way: from **positive to negative**.

cards.front: Trap: a question asks you to mark the negative terminal and the direction of electron flow. What is the safe check?
cards.back:
Electrons leave the **negative** terminal; conventional current arrows leave the **positive** one. The two are always opposite.

Examiners report both the terminal and the direction being confused.

cards.front: In the symbol for a cell, which line is the positive terminal?
cards.back:
The **long thin line** is positive; the short thick line is negative.

That is what cell polarity means, and it decides which way round the cell drives the current.

cards.front: Recall the standard symbols for a cell, switch, lamp, resistor, variable resistor, ammeter, voltmeter and fuse
cards.back: Cell: one long and one short line. Switch: a gap with a hinged blade. Lamp: a circle with a cross. Resistor: a plain rectangle. Variable resistor: a rectangle with an arrow through it. Ammeter and voltmeter: circles marked A and V. Fuse: a rectangle with a line through it.

image.alt: Eight standard circuit symbols in two rows, each with short connecting wires and a label: cell, switch, lamp, resistor on the top row; variable resistor, ammeter, voltmeter and fuse on the bottom row.
image.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 340 140' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.5'><path d='M16 34 L41 34 M53 34 L74 34 M41 27 L41 41 M53 21 L53 47'/><path d='M101 34 L116 34 M144 34 L159 34 M116 34 L142 24'/><circle cx='116' cy='34' r='2' fill='currentColor' stroke='none'/><circle cx='144' cy='34' r='2' fill='currentColor' stroke='none'/><path d='M186 34 L206 34 M224 34 L244 34'/><circle cx='215' cy='34' r='9'/><path d='M209 28 L221 40 M221 28 L209 40'/><path d='M271 34 L288 34 M312 34 L329 34'/><rect x='288' y='27' width='24' height='14'/><path d='M16 100 L33 100 M57 100 L74 100'/><rect x='33' y='93' width='24' height='14'/><path d='M28 114 L62 86 M54 86 L62 86 L62 94'/><path d='M101 100 L120 100 M140 100 L159 100'/><circle cx='130' cy='100' r='10'/><path d='M186 100 L205 100 M225 100 L244 100'/><circle cx='215' cy='100' r='10'/><path d='M271 100 L288 100 M312 100 L329 100'/><rect x='288' y='93' width='24' height='14'/><path d='M288 100 L312 100'/><g font-size='8' fill='currentColor' stroke='none'><text x='36' y='60'>cell</text><text x='116' y='60'>switch</text><text x='204' y='60'>lamp</text><text x='285' y='60'>resistor</text><text x='10' y='126'>variable resistor</text><text x='112' y='126'>ammeter</text><text x='196' y='126'>voltmeter</text><text x='292' y='126'>fuse</text><text x='126' y='104' font-size='11'>A</text><text x='211' y='104' font-size='11'>V</text></g></svg>

cards.front: Trap: which circuit symbol is most often drawn wrongly?
cards.back:
The **variable resistor** - candidates draw a switch or a plain fixed resistor instead.

It is a rectangle with an **arrow drawn diagonally through it**.
cards.source: CER Summer 2025 P2 (H); CER Summer 2023 U7B Physics (H)

cards.front: Where do an ammeter and a voltmeter go in a circuit?
cards.back:
**Ammeter in series**, in the main line, so the whole current passes through it.

**Voltmeter in parallel**, connected across the component whose voltage you want.

cards.front: Trap: a voltmeter is drawn in the main loop of a circuit. What is wrong?
cards.back:
A voltmeter must be **in parallel**, connected across the component.

Putting it in series is one of the most repeated circuit errors, and the whole circuit mark is lost.

cards.front: What does a switch do in a circuit?
cards.back: It **makes or breaks** the circuit: closed, the two terminals are connected and current flows; open, the contact is broken and it stops.

cards.front: An ____ has no free electrons, so charge cannot flow through it.
cards.back: **insulator**

topics.title: Charge, current and cells in series

cards.front: Equation linking charge, current and time
cards.back:
In words: charge = current x time.

In symbols: $Q = I \times t$

Units: Q in coulombs (C), I in amperes (A), t in **seconds**.

Rearranged: $I = \frac{Q}{t}$ and $t = \frac{Q}{I}$.

cards.front: Electric charge
cards.back:
Coulomb, symbol **C**.

One coulomb is the charge carried past a point in one second by a current of one ampere.

cards.front: Trap: a question gives a current of 250 mA for 2 minutes. What goes into Q = It?
cards.back:
**0.25 A** and **120 s**.

Divide milliamps by 1000 and multiply minutes by 60 before substituting - both conversions are repeatedly missed.

cards.front: A current of 0.5 A flows for 2 minutes. Charge?
cards.back:
**60 C**

2 minutes = 120 s, so $Q = 0.5 \times 120 = 60$ C

cards.front: 45 C of charge passes a point in 15 s. Current?
What voltage do cells in series provide?
cards.back:
The **sum of the voltages** of the separate cells, **taking their polarity into account**.

A cell connected the opposite way round subtracts from the total.

cards.front: Three 1.5 V cells in series, all facing the same way. Total voltage? And if one is reversed?

topics.title: Ohm's law, V = IR and the filament lamp

cards.front: Equation linking voltage, current and resistance
cards.back:
In words: voltage = current x resistance.

In symbols: $V = I \times R$

Units: V in volts (V), I in amperes (A), R in ohms.

Rearranged: $I = \frac{V}{R}$ and $R = \frac{V}{I}$.

cards.front: Trap: the current is given as 600 mA. What goes into V = IR?
cards.back:
**0.6 A** - divide milliamps by 1000.

This exact conversion is named in two separate reports as the reason otherwise correct methods scored nothing.

cards.front: State Ohm's law
cards.back: At a **constant temperature**, the **current** through a conductor is **directly proportional to the voltage** across it.

cards.front: What does the V-I graph for a metal wire at constant temperature look like, and how are the axes set out?
cards.back:
A **straight line through the origin**, with **voltage on the y-axis** and **current on the x-axis**.

The straight line through the origin is what shows that current and voltage are proportional.

cards.front: Prescribed Practical P6: the V-I characteristic of a metal wire
cards.back:
1 Connect the wire, a cell, a **switch**, a **variable resistor** and an **ammeter in series**.
2 Connect a **voltmeter in parallel** across the wire.
3 Use the variable resistor for a good spread of readings.
4 Keep the currents small and switch off between readings, so the temperature stays constant.
5 Plot voltage (y) against current (x); draw the best-fit line.

cards.front: Trap: why is the wire switched off between readings and kept at small currents?
cards.back:
To hold the **temperature constant**. Ohm's law only applies at constant temperature; if the wire warms up its resistance rises and the graph bends.

Temperature is the control variable examiners look for.

cards.front: Higher: what shape is the V-I graph for a filament lamp?
cards.back:
A **curve**, not a straight line: as the current rises, the voltage has to rise by more and more for each extra amp.

That shows the **resistance is increasing**.

cards.front: Trap: explain fully why the filament lamp's V-I graph curves
cards.back:
Current increases, so the filament gets **hotter**; its ions **vibrate more**; the free electrons **collide with them more often**; the **resistance increases**.

Saying only that the resistance rises, without the temperature and collisions, does not get full marks.

cards.front: Higher: show from a filament lamp graph that the resistance increases
cards.back:
1 Choose a point low on the curve; read its V and I.
2 Work out $R = \frac{V}{I}$ at that point.
3 Repeat at a point higher up the curve.
4 Compare: the ratio V/I is **larger** at the higher current, so the resistance has increased.

cards.front: V = 6 V across a resistor carrying 0.4 A. Resistance?
A 20 ohm resistor carries 600 mA. Voltage across it?
cards.back:
**12 V**

600 mA = 0.6 A, so $V = I \times R = 0.6 \times 20 = 12$ V

cards.front: Trap: the plotted points of a filament lamp characteristic are joined with a ruler. What is lost?
cards.back:
The line mark. Draw a **smooth best-fit curve** through the points.

Ruled lines between points, and axis labels without units, are the usual graph losses in this practical.

topics.title: Current and voltage rules in series and parallel circuits

cards.front: What is the rule for the current in a series circuit?
cards.back:
The current through **each component is the same**, and it is the same at every point in the loop.

There is only one path, so the charge has nowhere else to go.

image.alt: Left: a series circuit with a cell and two lamps in a single loop. Right: a parallel circuit with a cell on the left-hand wire and two lamps on separate branches.

cards.front: What is the rule for the voltages in a series circuit?
cards.back: The **voltage of the supply equals the sum of the voltages** across the separate components.

cards.front: What is the rule for the voltage in a parallel circuit?
cards.back: The voltage across **each branch is the same** as the voltage of the supply.

cards.front: What is the rule for the currents in a parallel circuit?
cards.back: The **total current from the supply is the sum of the currents** in the separate branches.

cards.front: Two lamps are in series across a 6 V supply. There is 2.5 V across the first. Voltage across the second?
cards.back:
**3.5 V**

6 - 2.5 = 3.5 V, because the supply voltage is shared between the components.

cards.front: Two parallel branches draw 0.3 A and 0.5 A. Current from the supply?
cards.back:
**0.8 A**

The branch currents add up to the total taken from the supply.

cards.front: One lamp fails. What happens in a series circuit, and in a parallel circuit?
cards.back:
**Series**: the circuit is broken, so everything goes out.

**Parallel**: only that branch stops; the others still have the full supply voltage and keep working.

cards.front: In a ____ circuit the current is the same at every point, and the supply voltage is shared between the components.
cards.back: **series**

topics.title: Calculating combined resistance

cards.front: Equation for resistors in series
cards.back:
In words: total resistance = the sum of the separate resistances.

In symbols: $R = R_1 + R_2$ (and so on).

The total is always **larger** than any one of them.

cards.front: A 12 ohm and an 8 ohm resistor in series. Total resistance?
Equation for two equal resistors in parallel
cards.back:
In words: the combined resistance is **half the resistance of one** of them.

In symbols: $R = \frac{R_1}{2}$

The two paths let twice as much current flow for the same voltage.

cards.front: Two 9 ohm resistors in parallel. Combined resistance?
cards.back:
**4.5 ohms**

$R = \frac{9}{2} = 4.5$. Examiners report that this exact answer was widely missed.

cards.front: Trap: your parallel answer is bigger than both resistors. What has gone wrong?
cards.back:
The combined resistance of a parallel pair is **always smaller than the smaller resistor**, because you have added another path for the current.

An answer larger than either one is a sure sign of an arithmetic slip.

cards.front: Higher: equation for any two resistors in parallel
cards.back:
$\frac{1}{R} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2}$

Or use the product over the sum: $R = \frac{R_1 R_2}{R_1 + R_2}$.

Resistances in ohms.

cards.front: Higher trap: you work out 1/R = 0.25 and write R = 0.25 ohms. What is missing?
cards.back:
The **final reciprocal**. If $\frac{1}{R} = 0.25$ then $R = \frac{1}{0.25} = 4$ ohms.

Forgetting to invert at the end turns a correct method into a wrong answer.

cards.front: Higher: 4 ohm and 12 ohm resistors in parallel. Combined resistance?
Higher: 2 ohm and 3 ohm resistors in parallel. Combined resistance?
Higher: find the total resistance of a circuit with series and parallel sections
cards.back:
1 Find the **parallel** section first and replace it with its single combined value.
2 Redraw the circuit with that one resistor in place.
3 **Add** the remaining resistances in series.
4 Use $V = IR$ with the total if the question then asks for a current.

cards.front: Higher: a 6 ohm resistor in series with two 4 ohm resistors that are in parallel. Total resistance?
cards.back:
**8 ohms**

Parallel pair first: $\frac{4}{2} = 2$ ohms. Then in series: 6 + 2 = 8 ohms.

topics.title: Resistance and length of a wire; the heating effect of a current

cards.front: How does the resistance of a metal wire at constant temperature depend on its length?
cards.back:
They are **proportional**: the resistance (y) against length (x) graph is a **straight line that passes through the origin**.

Double the length, double the resistance.

cards.front: Investigate how the resistance of a wire depends on its length
cards.back:
1 Clamp a long uniform wire beside a metre rule.
2 Connect a fixed length into the circuit, or use an ohmmeter across it.
3 Measure the resistance (or V and I, then $R = \frac{V}{I}$).
4 Repeat for at least six different lengths.
5 Plot resistance (y) against length (x) and draw the best-fit line.

cards.front: Trap: a student gives 'length' as a control variable in the resistance-length experiment. Why is that wrong?
cards.back:
Length is the **independent variable** - the thing you deliberately change.

The **controls** are the **thickness (diameter)** of the wire, the **material** and the **temperature**.

cards.front: The gradient of a resistance-length graph
cards.back:
**Ohms per metre**, or ohms per centimetre if the length axis is in cm.

A gradient without its unit loses a mark.

cards.front: Why does a current heat up a metal wire?
cards.back:
The **free electrons collide with the atoms (ions)** of the metal as they move through it, **transferring energy** to them.

The atoms vibrate more, so the wire gets hotter.

cards.front: 2 m of a wire has a resistance of 6 ohms. Resistance of 5 m of the same wire?
cards.back:
**15 ohms**

6 / 2 = 3 ohms per metre, so 5 x 3 = 15 ohms.

cards.front: Doubling the length of a wire at constant temperature ____ its resistance.
cards.back: **doubles**

cards.front: Trap: what does a graph have to show before you may write 'directly proportional'?
cards.back:
A **straight line that passes through the origin**.

A straight line that misses the origin, or a curve, shows the quantities are related but **not** proportional.

topics.title: Electrical energy, power and the cost of electricity

cards.front: Equation for electrical energy transferred
cards.back:
In words: energy = power x time.

In symbols: $E = P \times t$

Units: E in joules (J), P in watts (W), t in **seconds**.

Rearranged: $P = \frac{E}{t}$ and $t = \frac{E}{P}$.

cards.front: Equation for electrical power
cards.back:
In words: power = current x voltage.

In symbols: $P = I \times V$

Units: P in watts (W), I in amperes (A), V in volts (V).

Rearranged: $I = \frac{P}{V}$ and $V = \frac{P}{I}$.

cards.front: Trap: an appliance runs for 10 minutes. What two things do candidates get wrong here?
cards.back:
They fail to recall **P = I x V**, and they leave the time in minutes.

For joules the time must be in **seconds**: 10 minutes = 600 s.

cards.front: A 2 kW heater runs for 10 minutes. Energy transferred in joules?
A device draws 3 A from the 230 V mains. Power?
cards.back:
**690 W**

$P = I \times V = 3 \times 230 = 690$ W

cards.front: Define the kilowatt-hour
cards.back:
The amount of **electrical energy used by a device of power 1000 W in one hour**.

It is the 'unit' of electricity that appears on a bill.

cards.front: Equation for the cost of electricity
cards.back:
energy (kWh) = power (**kW**) x time (**hours**)
cost = number of kWh x price per unit

For kilowatt-hours, use kilowatts and hours - never watts and seconds.

cards.front: A 2.5 kW appliance runs for 4 hours. Units used, and cost at 30p per unit?
A 100 W lamp is left on for 20 hours. Units of electricity used?
Trap: which units go with joules, and which with kilowatt-hours?
cards.back:
**Joules**: watts and **seconds** ($E = Pt$).
**Kilowatt-hours**: kilowatts and **hours**.

Mixing the two - for example watts with hours - is the classic slip in a cost question.

topics.title: a.c. and d.c., switching, plugs, fuses, earthing and double insulation

cards.front: Define direct current
cards.back:
Current which **always flows in the same direction**.

Cells and batteries give d.c.

cards.front: Define alternating current
cards.back:
Current which **changes direction periodically**.

The mains supply is a.c.

cards.front: How do you recognise a.c. and d.c. from a cathode ray oscilloscope trace?
cards.back:
**d.c.**: a straight horizontal line, above (or below) the centre line.

**a.c.**: a repeating wave that goes above and below the centre line, because the current keeps reversing.

cards.front: Where must a one-way switch be placed, and what does it do?
cards.back:
On the **live** side of the circuit.

It is a make-or-break switch: turned on, the two terminals are connected; turned off, the contact between them is broken and the appliance is isolated from the live wire.

cards.front: Name the three wires in a fused three-pin plug, with their colours and positions
cards.back:
**Live**: brown, on the **right**, and it goes through the **fuse**.
**Neutral**: blue, on the **left**.
**Earth**: green and yellow, the **top (longest) pin**, connected to the metal case.

image.alt: A three-pin plug seen from the inside. The longest pin at the top is the earth, the pin on the left is the neutral and the pin on the right is the live, which is wired through a fuse. The three wires run from the cable grip at the bottom to their terminals.

cards.front: Explain how the earth wire and the fuse protect the user together
cards.back:
1 The live wire comes loose and touches the **metal case**.
2 The case is joined to **earth**, a very low-resistance path.
3 A **very large current** flows to earth.
4 It **melts the fuse** in the live wire.
5 The circuit is **broken**, so the case is no longer live.

cards.front: Define double insulation
cards.back: When an appliance has **all its live internal components completely encased in an insulator**, usually a plastic case.

cards.front: Why does a double-insulated appliance not need an earth wire?
cards.back: There is **no metal case** for a loose live wire to make live. The plastic casing is an insulator, so the user can never touch a conducting part that is connected to the live wire.

cards.front: Choose the right fuse for an appliance
cards.back:
1 Work out the normal operating current: $I = \frac{P}{V}$ with V = 230 V for the mains.
2 Pick the **smallest standard fuse rated above** that current.
3 The standard ratings are **3 A, 5 A and 13 A**.
4 A fuse just above the working current still blows quickly in a fault.

cards.front: A 920 W appliance on the 230 V mains. Which fuse?
cards.back:
**5 A**

$I = \frac{920}{230} = 4$ A, so the next standard rating above 4 A is 5 A.

cards.front: A 2300 W kettle on the 230 V mains. Which fuse?
cards.back:
**13 A**

$I = \frac{2300}{230} = 10$ A, so the 13 A fuse is the smallest standard rating above it.

cards.front: Trap: 'the fuse takes the extra current away'. What actually happens?
cards.back:
The fuse is a thin wire in the **live** side that **melts** when the current gets too big, **breaking the circuit** and cutting off the supply.

Fuse action in a plug was the least well answered part of a whole P2 paper.

cards.front: Trap: why is a 13 A fuse a poor choice for a 60 W lamp?
cards.back:
The lamp only draws about 0.26 A, so a fault current well below 13 A would never melt the fuse - the flex could overheat first.

Always choose the smallest standard rating **just above** the normal current.

topics.title: Magnetic fields of bar magnets and coils; electromagnets

cards.front: Describe the shape and direction of the magnetic field around a bar magnet
cards.back:
Curved loops that leave the **north pole**, spread out around the magnet and return to the **south pole**.

The arrows run **from north to south outside the magnet**, and the lines are **closest together at the poles**.

image.alt: A bar magnet with its north pole on the left and south pole on the right, surrounded by curved magnetic field lines that leave the north pole, loop above and below the magnet and enter the south pole, each carrying an arrow pointing from north to south.

cards.front: Plot the magnetic field of a bar magnet with a plotting compass
cards.back:
1 Lay the magnet on paper and draw round it.
2 Put the compass near one pole; dot each end of the needle.
3 Move the compass so its tail sits on the last dot, and dot the new head.
4 Repeat to the other pole, then join the dots smoothly.
5 Arrow the line the way the needle pointed.

cards.front: What is the shape of the field produced by a current in a coil of wire?
cards.back:
Outside the coil it looks just like the field of a **bar magnet**, with a north pole at one end and a south pole at the other.

Inside the coil the field lines are straight and close together.

cards.front: What happens to the poles of a coil if the current is reversed?
cards.back:
The **poles swap over**: the end that was north becomes south.

The polarity of a coil depends on the direction of the current in it.

cards.front: What three things make an electromagnet stronger?
cards.back: A larger **current** in the coil, a greater **number of turns** on the coil, and a **soft iron core** instead of air.

cards.front: Trap: to test what makes an electromagnet stronger, a student changes the battery or the size of the core. Why is that not what was asked?
cards.back:
The three variables on this specification are the **current**, the **number of turns** and the **material of the core**.

Changing the battery or the core's dimensions is not one of them, and the answer scores nothing.

cards.front: Investigate how the strength of an electromagnet depends on the current
cards.back:
1 Wind a fixed number of turns onto an iron core.
2 Connect the coil, an ammeter and a variable resistor in series.
3 Set a current and count how many paper clips the electromagnet holds.
4 Repeat for several currents, keeping the turns and the core the same.
5 Plot paper clips held against current.

cards.front: Magnetic field lines are closest together where the field is ____.
cards.back:
**strongest**

That is why they are packed together at the poles of a bar magnet.

topics.title: The Solar System, orbits and artificial satellites

cards.front: Name the main features of the Solar System
cards.back: The **Sun**, the **rocky planets** and the **gas planets**, their **moons**, and the **asteroids** and **comets**.

cards.front: List the eight planets in order from the Sun outwards
cards.back:
Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.

The first four are the rocky planets; the last four are the gas planets.

cards.front: What provides the force needed for orbital motion?
cards.back: **Gravity** - for planets, comets, moons and artificial satellites alike.

cards.front: Trap: 'the Sun pushes the planets around their orbits'. What is wrong?
cards.back:
Gravity is always a **pull**, an attraction towards the Sun - never a push.

Describing gravity as a push is named in the reports for both the Solar System and the stars questions.

cards.front: Trap: a question asks which objects orbit the Sun. Do meteors and meteorites count here?
cards.back:
**No.** The objects this specification names as orbiting the Sun are the **planets, asteroids and comets** (with moons orbiting planets).

Candidates lost marks by listing meteors and meteorites.

cards.front: Trap: where does the Sun go on a Solar System diagram?
cards.back:
At the **centre**, with the planets in orbit around it in order outwards.

Drawing the Sun to one side, as though the planets were in a line beside it, lost marks in Summer 2025.

cards.front: Define an artificial satellite
cards.back: A **man-made** satellite that has been **launched into space** and is held in orbit by gravity.

cards.front: Give the four uses of artificial satellites named in this specification
cards.back: **Observation of the Earth**, **weather monitoring**, **astronomy** and **communications**.

cards.front: A moon orbits a planet, and a planet orbits the Sun; in both cases the force needed is provided by ____.
cards.back: **gravity**

topics.title: Formation of stars and planets; fusion in stars

cards.front: How does a star form?
cards.back: Enough **dust and gas from space** is **pulled together by gravitational attraction** until it forms a star.

cards.front: How do planets form alongside a star?
cards.back: **Smaller masses** of dust and gas also come together, and are then **attracted by the larger mass** of the star, so they become planets in orbit around it.

cards.front: Trap: in the six-mark stars question, how must gravity be described?
cards.back:
As an **attraction that pulls** dust and gas together.

'Gravity pushes the material together' was a marked-down answer in Summer 2025.

cards.front: What are stars made of, and how is that known?
cards.back:
Mainly **hydrogen and helium**.

**Studies of the light from stars**, including the Sun, show which elements are present.

cards.front: Trap: 'we know because scientists study the light from stars'. What is missing?
cards.back:
**What the light shows**: that stars are made mainly of hydrogen and helium.

Examiners report that the evidence was named but never explained.

cards.front: Where does a star's energy come from?
cards.back: The **fusion of hydrogen into helium** in its core.

cards.front: Higher: where did the naturally occurring elements come from?
cards.back: All of them **except hydrogen** were formed by **nuclear fusion in stars**.

cards.front: A star forms when enough dust and gas is pulled together by ____ ____.
cards.back: **gravitational attraction**

topics.title: Life cycles of stars, supernovae and black holes

cards.front: Higher: give the life cycle of a star with the mass of our Sun
cards.back: **Protostar, main sequence, red giant, white dwarf, black dwarf.**

cards.front: Higher: why is a star stable during its main sequence period?
cards.back: The **outward force of thermal expansion** is **balanced by the inward force of gravity**.

cards.front: Higher: what happens to a much more massive star after the main sequence?
cards.back: It becomes a **red supergiant**, then explodes as a **supernova**, in which the **outer layers of the star are ejected**.

cards.front: Higher: how bright is a supernova, and for how long?
cards.back: It shines with the brightness of about **10 billion suns**, for a **relatively short time**.

cards.front: Higher: what is left after a supernova?
cards.back: The remaining **core collapses further**. Some become **neutron stars**; the **very most massive** form **black holes**.

cards.front: Higher: define a black hole
cards.back: What is left after a very massive star completes a supernova: its **gravitational field is so strong that nothing can escape from it**, including electromagnetic radiation such as light.

cards.front: Higher trap: will the Sun end its life as a supernova?
cards.back:
**No.** A supernova needs a **much more massive** star.

The Sun follows the low-mass route: red giant, then white dwarf, then black dwarf.

cards.front: Higher: sort the two star routes when a question mixes the stages
cards.back:
1 Both start as a **protostar** and then a **main sequence** star.
2 Sun-like mass: red giant, **white dwarf**, black dwarf.
3 Much greater mass: **red supergiant**, supernova, then neutron star or black hole.
4 Check the words: 'giant' and 'dwarf' belong to the Sun-like route, 'supergiant' to the massive one.

cards.front: Higher: after its red giant stage, a star like the Sun becomes a white dwarf and finally a ____ ____.
cards.back: **black dwarf**

topics.title: The Big Bang, red shift and CMBR

cards.front: How did the Universe begin, and how long ago?
cards.back: With the **Big Bang**, which according to current measurements happened about **14 billion years ago**.

cards.front: What is red shift?
cards.back: Light from **other galaxies** is **shifted towards the red end of the spectrum**.

cards.front: How is red shift explained, and why is it evidence for the Big Bang?
cards.back:
It is explained by **space expanding**, which stretches the light on its way to us.

An expanding Universe is what the Big Bang model predicts.

cards.front: Light reaching us from distant galaxies is shifted towards the ____ end of the spectrum.
cards.back: **red**

cards.front: Higher: what happened in the first stage of the Big Bang model?
cards.back: **Rapid expansion and cooling** of the Universe.

cards.front: Higher: what formed as the Universe cooled, in order?
cards.back: First **neutrons and protons**; further expansion and cooling let **nuclei** form; more cooling still let **electrons combine with nuclei** to form **atoms of hydrogen**.

cards.front: Higher: set out the Big Bang model in order
cards.back:
1 A Big Bang, then **rapid expansion and cooling**.
2 **Neutrons and protons** form.
3 Further expansion and cooling lets **nuclei** form.
4 More cooling lets **electrons** combine with nuclei.
5 **Hydrogen atoms** form.

cards.front: Higher: what is cosmic microwave background radiation?
cards.back:
**Radiation left over from the Big Bang**, spread across the whole sky.

It is further evidence for the Big Bang.
keyWords: left over from the Big Bang

cards.front: Higher trap: is CMBR the light we receive from stars?
cards.back:
**No.** It is microwave radiation **left over from the Big Bang** itself, not light from stars or galaxies.

Examiners report exactly this confusion at Higher Tier.

cards.front: Higher: why is CMBR such strong evidence for the Big Bang?
cards.back: The Big Bang is **currently the only model that explains** the existence of cosmic microwave background radiation.

cards.front: Name the two pieces of evidence for the Big Bang on this specification
cards.back: **Red shift** of the light from other galaxies, explained by space expanding, and (Higher Tier) **cosmic microwave background radiation**.
